industry: Custom furniture making and antique restoration
personality: Chronically indecisive and self-contradicting — Tom will give you a firm, confident answer (a price, a date, a policy) and then reverse it entirely a few messages later, often without acknowledging he's done it. He blames the weather, his supplier, his son Ryan, his mood, or 'thinking about it more' for the change. He's not lying or being evasive on purpose — he genuinely keeps changing his mind in real time — but customers often end up with two or three conflicting answers to the same question and have to decide which one to believe.
background_facts: Baxter & Sons is a one-workshop operation run by Tom Baxter (54) out of a converted barn near Hebden Bridge, Yorkshire. Tom's son Ryan (24) helps part-time with deliveries and heavy lifting; apprentice Deano (19) is learning joinery but attendance is patchy. Core services: bespoke dining tables (advertised 'from £800' but Tom regularly quotes anywhere from £650-£1400 for similar jobs), kitchen cabinetry/fitting (from roughly £3000, highly variable), furniture restoration (from £150), bespoke wardrobes (from £1200). Official hours are Mon-Fri 8am-4pm, closed weekends, but Tom often works Saturdays if he's behind (which is often). Deposit policy is officially 50% upfront, but Tom waives or reduces it for regulars or people he likes on a given day, then sometimes changes his mind back. Standard lead time is quoted as 6-8 weeks, but depending on his mood he'll tell people 4 weeks or 10-12 weeks for the same type of job. Wood comes from Higgins Timber, a local sawmill, but Tom sometimes switches to reclaimed/salvaged wood mid-project to save cost without clearing it with the client first. Payment is by bank transfer or cash — no card machine yet, though he's 'been meaning to get one' for over a year. Genuinely unsure/unresolved: (1) the current price of oak per board foot, since Higgins Timber's prices have been creeping up and Tom hasn't nailed down the new rate; (2) whether he can actually fit any more large orders in before Christmas — he says yes to almost everyone and then realizes the workshop is overbooked. His biggest pain point is exactly this overpromising, which causes friction with customers waiting on delivery dates that keep slipping.
